items.prompt: Priya knows the merge is happening but not which roles go. What should she do with those two facts?
choices: Hold both back until HR has finalized everything and it is safe
Call all of it undecided so nobody feels misled if details change
Say the merge is decided and the role list is not
items.explanation: Naming the decided part and the open part separately is the honest, useful version.

items.prompt: What does a 'known / unknown split' mean?
choices: Saying plainly what is locked and what is still open
Telling half the team now and the other half later
Guessing at the open part and presenting the guess as fact
items.explanation: It is a statement about the situation, not about who hears it.

items.prompt: Which sentence blurs known and unknown?
choices: The merge is decided but the names are not
Some changes may be coming at some point
HR will share the names this Friday at two
items.explanation: The vague sentence hides that part of the situation is already settled.

items.prompt: Why say out loud that the merge is decided?
choices: It lets Priya avoid follow-up questions
It guarantees nobody will lose a job
It gives the team one solid fact to stand on while the rest stays open
items.explanation: A confirmed fact reduces the sense that everything is unknown.

items.prompt: Which of these is still unknown for Priya?
choices: Which five people are affected
That the teams will merge
That the final team has ten people
items.explanation: Who is affected is exactly what HR has not finalized.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if Priya treats the open part as settled too?
choices: The team asks fewer questions from then on
She may state something that later changes
HR finishes its work noticeably faster
items.explanation: Announcing a maybe as a fact weakens her word when it moves.

items.prompt: A manager says 'a few things are in flux.' What is missing?
choices: A clear line between decided and open
A detailed review of the company's finances and budget
An apology for the stress the news will cause the team
items.explanation: The sentence names neither the settled part nor the open part.

items.prompt: Which is the best answer to 'what do you know so far?'
choices: Nothing that I am able to share yet
Everything is still being worked out by leadership
The merge is happening, the role list is not final
items.explanation: It gives both halves, briefly and honestly.

items.prompt: Priya has three facts: the merge is approved, five roles will go, and HR has not chosen which. A teammate asks what is settled. Which reply keeps the split honest?
choices: The merge is settled, but the count of five could still change later
The merge and the affected roles are settled; only timing is open
Everything depends on HR, so none of it is truly settled yet
The merge and the count of five are settled; only who is affected is open
items.explanation: The count was confirmed by her director, so it belongs on the decided side. Only the names are open. The other replies drop a settled fact or invent one.
items.reference:
Decided vs. open
decided: the merge, 15 to 10
open: which 5 roles, until HR finalizes
known: the date names will exist
Why: naming both halves plainly stops a partly settled situation from reading as one giant unknown.
items.learnMore:
Splitting known from unknown

A change is rarely all decided or all open. Saying which part is which keeps the settled part credible while being honest about the rest.

Common mistake

Saying 'some changes are coming', which makes even the locked part sound shaky.
items.reflection: Think of a change you lived through at work or school. Which part was already decided, and which part was only rumored?

It names a date that the manager cannot yet guarantee to anyone
It leaves out an apology for the worry that the news will cause
items.explanation: The statement is too vague, not too detailed: it gives the settled fact the same fog as the open ones. Honest does not require sharing names, only separating the halves.

I don't know yet, and I will tell you the day I do

items.prompt: What is false reassurance?

A promise to share updates with the team as they come in
Any kind words offered during a hard moment for the team
items.explanation: The problem is the missing standing, not the kindness.

It damages trust in her word on later topics too
It shortens the meeting and so saves everyone time

choices: I am sure no one on this team is going to be affected
Leadership would never cut a team that performs like ours does
I have not seen a list and nobody has been ranked so far
items.explanation: It is true and checkable, which is what standing means.

items.prompt: Is 'I don't know' a dodge?
choices: No, when true and paired with what she does know
Only when a date for the next update follows it directly
Yes, since any admission of not knowing undermines a leader
items.explanation: Declining to promise is not the same as declining to answer.

items.prompt: The team wants comfort. What can Priya offer honestly?

Her commitment to tell them the same day she hears
A promise that things will certainly turn out fine
items.explanation: A commitment about her own behavior is something she controls.

items.prompt: How far does the damage of a broken reassurance reach?
choices: To her word on later hard conversations
Only to the one person affected
Nowhere, if the news is delivered kindly
items.explanation: The team learns her reassurances are not reliable.

items.prompt: Priya says 'I'd rather you trust me than feel better today.' What is she doing?
choices: Refusing to discuss the topic with her team at all
Passing the blame for the situation up to HR and leadership
Trading brief comfort for lasting credibility
items.explanation: She chooses durable trust over a short-term good feeling.

items.prompt: A manager says 'I really don't think anyone here is at risk' before roles are chosen. One person is later laid off. Which describes the added damage best?
choices: The layoff arrives sooner than it would have otherwise
The team doubts her reassurances on every later topic
The affected person loses severance they would otherwise have received
The manager is blamed for the budget cut that caused the layoffs
items.explanation: The layoff was coming regardless. What the false claim adds is a record of the manager being wrong in the reassuring direction, which taxes later trust.
items.reference:
Reassurance vs. honesty
'you're safe' (no standing): breaks if wrong
'no list yet, same-day news' (true): holds either way
cost of a broken promise: your word
Why: a comfort you cannot guarantee costs more later than the discomfort it avoids today.
items.learnMore:
The standing to promise

You can only promise what you control or know. Anything else is a hope, and presenting hope as a promise spends your credibility.

Common mistake

Treating 'I don't know' as a dodge, when it is the most accurate answer available.
items.reflection: When did someone reassure you about something they could not have known? How did it affect how you took their next statement?

items.prompt: Two managers face the same nine-day wait. One says 'you'll hear when I know.' The other says 'you'll hear Friday, whatever the news.' What is the main practical difference?

The second guarantees better news than the first can promise
The first is more honest because it avoids naming a day
The first reduces how often the team asks for updates
items.explanation: Information is identical, but the date turns an open wait into a bounded one and commits the manager to showing up.
items.reference:
Open vs. bounded wait
'soon' / 'when I know': no edge
'Friday, whatever the news': an edge
same information, very different feeling
Why: a named date turns an unbounded wait into a bounded one, which is easier to carry.
items.learnMore:
The power of a date

People tolerate waiting better when they know when it ends. A specific day also creates accountability: the manager has to show up, even with nothing new.

Common mistake

Promising 'as soon as I know' and calling that a date.

Why silence is never empty

Teams interpret missing information as a signal. The longer the gap and the stronger the leaked signal, the more the guesses dominate.

items.prompt: A director says a merger is 'likely' but not approved. No one outside leadership knows. A manager is tempted to prepare the team. Which is the best move?

items.reference:
Timing tree
not decided: wait, don't announce a maybe
decided, no leak: tell them soon
decided + leaked: tell them today
Why: the right moment depends on whether it is decided and whether the rumor has already started.
items.learnMore:
Timing is its own decision

Wording and timing are separate choices. Announce too early and 'confirmed' loses meaning; too late and you are correcting a story instead of telling one.
